transcript.text: my belling cooker keeps burnin stuff 1 day then next day its undercookd on same temp. been like it a cuple months. thermastat??

It sounds incredibly frustrating to deal with inconsistent cooking results, especially when you’re trying to rely on your oven for daily meals. You are likely correct in suspecting the thermostat (or more accurately, the temperature sensor and control board), but there are a few other common culprits that could be causing this "hot one day, cold the next" behavior.

Here’s a breakdown of what might be going wrong and how to troubleshoot it:

### 1. The Temperature Sensor (Thermistor)
This is the most likely cause if the temperature fluctuates wildly between days.
• What it does: A small probe inside the oven wall measures the actual air temperature and sends data to the control board.
• The problem: If the sensor is failing, corroded, or out of calibration, it might read "180°C" when it’s actually 220°C (burning food) one day, and then read "180°C" when it’s only 150°C (undercooking) the next.
• Test: You can buy an oven thermometer (cheap and available at most kitchen stores). Place it in the center of the oven on the middle rack. Preheat to a standard temperature (e.g., 180°C/350°F). After 20 minutes, check the reading. If it’s off by more than 10–15 degrees, your sensor or calibration is off.

### 2. Faulty Heating Element
• Top/Broil Element: If this element is sticking "on" too long or not cycling properly, you’ll get burning on top while the inside remains undercooked.
• Bottom/Roasting Element: If this isn’t heating enough, your food will be undercooked.
• Test: Visually inspect both elements for blistering, holes, or signs of wear. Also, listen to the oven cycle. It should click on and off periodically as it maintains temperature. If it stays on continuously without cycling, the element or control board may be faulty.

### 3. Calibration Issue
• Many modern ovens allow you to adjust the temperature calibration (offset). Over time, the factory setting can drift.
• Solution: Check your oven’s manual for a "calibration" or "temperature offset" setting in the menu. You might be able to adjust it by +10°F or -10°F to correct the bias.

### 4. Faulty Control Board (Electronic Oven Control)
• If the sensor is fine but the oven still behaves erratically, the brain of the oven (the control board) may be sending incorrect signals to the heating elements. This can cause random overheating or underheating.
• Signs: Error codes on the display, unresponsive buttons, or the behavior described above despite a correct sensor reading.

### 5. Door Seal (Gasket) Issues
• If the rubber seal around the door is cracked, torn, or dirty, heat escapes. This can cause the oven to work harder and cycle irregularly, leading to uneven cooking.
• Test: Close the door on a dollar bill. If it slides out easily when you pull it, your seal is loose and needs replacement.

---

### ✅ Recommended Next Steps:

1.  Buy an Oven Thermometer: This is the cheapest and most definitive way to diagnose the problem. Use it for 2–3 days at different times of day.
• If the thermometer shows consistent but wrong temps → Calibration issue.
• If the thermometer shows wildly fluctuating temps (e.g., 160°C one hour, 200°C the next) → Faulty sensor or control board.

2.  Check the Door Seal: Clean it thoroughly and check for gaps.

3.  Consult a Technician:
• If your oven is under warranty, contact the manufacturer.
• If not, a technician can test the resistance of the temperature sensor with a multimeter to confirm if it’s faulty. Replacing a sensor is usually inexpensive ($20–$50 for parts + labor).

### ⚠️ Safety Note:
If your oven is burning food consistently, there may be an electrical fault causing overheating. If you smell burning plastic or see sparks, unplug the oven and call a professional immediately.

That detail about the orange light is actually very helpful! It tells us exactly how your oven works.

Since you have knobs and a simple indicator light, your oven likely uses a mechanical thermostat (a bimetallic strip) rather than digital electronics. Here’s what that means:

### What the Light Tells Us
• Light ON: The heating element is actively heating up.
• Light OFF: The thermostat has reached the set temperature and cut power to the element to let it cool down slightly before turning back on. This "cycling" keeps the oven at a steady temp.

### Why It’s Inconsistent
If the light stays on for ages one day (burning food) but turns off quickly the next (undercooking), it suggests the thermostat is failing to cycle correctly.

Here are the most likely causes:

1.  The Thermostat is Failing: The internal mechanism that senses temperature might be worn out or sticking. It might not "feel" that the oven is hot enough, so it keeps the element on too long (burning). Or, it might think it’s reached temp when it hasn’t, cutting power too early (undercooking).
2.  The Heating Element is Failing: If the element itself is degrading, it might heat up very slowly or unevenly. This can confuse the thermostat about whether the oven has reached the target temperature.

### What You Can Do Now (Without a Thermometer)

1.  Check for "Cold Spots": Try baking something simple like cookies or toast on different racks and in different corners of the oven. If one side consistently burns while another undercooks, it’s likely an element issue (e.g., the top element is stuck on).
2.  Listen to the Cycle: Turn the oven on to a medium heat (like 180°C/350°F). Watch and listen for about 20–30 minutes.
• Does the light turn off?
• Does it turn back on again after a few minutes?
• If it stays ON continuously for more than 10–15 minutes without turning off, your thermostat is likely stuck "on."
• If it turns off but never turns back on (and the oven gets cold), the thermostat might be stuck "off."

### The Fix
Since this has been happening for a couple of months and involves a core safety/temperature component, you’ll likely need to replace either the thermostat or the heating element.

• Thermostat Replacement: Usually located behind the control knobs. It’s often a simple DIY job if you’re comfortable with basic tools (unplug the oven first!).
• Heating Element Replacement: Also usually accessible from inside the oven cavity.

Recommendation: Given that this is an electrical appliance and inconsistent heating can be a fire hazard, I’d suggest calling a qualified appliance repair technician to diagnose whether it’s the thermostat or element. They can test both with a multimeter to confirm which part is faulty before you replace anything.
